title: Der Bauer und der Teufel
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 189. Text from Wikisource („Der Bauer und der Teufel (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: A shrewd peasant finds the devil sitting on a buried treasure and strikes a bargain to split his harvest with him for two years. By choosing turnips the first year and offering the devil only the leaves, then wheat the second year and offering him only the stubble, the peasant keeps the useful half of each crop for himself both times. It is a trickster tale in the oldest sense, the weak outwitting the strong by knowing exactly what is being asked.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein kluges und verschmitztes Bäuerlein, von dessen Streichen viel zu erzählen wäre: die schönste Geschichte ist aber doch, wie er den Teufel einmal dran gekriegt und zum Narren gehabt hat.
sentences.l: There was once a clever and sly little-peasant, of whose tricks there would be much to tell: the finest story is however this, how he once caught the devil out and had him for a fool.
sentences.i: There was once a clever, sly little peasant of whose tricks there would be much to tell; but the finest story of all is how he once caught the devil out and made a fool of him.
sentences.n: verschmitzt is sly in an admiring way — the tale takes the peasant’s side in its first line. jemanden dran kriegen is to catch someone out, get the better of him; jemanden zum Narren haben is to make a fool of him, and Narren there is the singular Narr inside a fixed phrase, not a plural. wäre is subjunctive: there would be much to tell, if one were telling it.

sentences.t: Das Bäuerlein hatte eines Tages seinen Acker bestellt und rüstete sich zur Heimfahrt als die Dämmerung schon eingetreten war.
sentences.l: The little-peasant had one day his field tilled and made himself ready for the journey home as the twilight had already set in.
sentences.i: One day the little peasant had worked his field and was making ready to drive home, when the dusk had already come on.
sentences.n: eines Tages is the genitive of time — literally “of a day”, meaning one day; German reaches for it constantly. den Acker bestellen is to till or work a field, nothing to do with ordering. sich rüsten is to get oneself ready.

sentences.t: Da erblickte er mitten auf seinem Acker einen Haufen feuriger Kohlen, und als er voll Verwunderung hinzugieng, so saß oben auf der Glut ein kleiner schwarzer Teufel.
sentences.l: Then caught he sight, in the middle of his field, of a heap of fiery coals, and as he full of wonder went up to it, there sat on top of the embers a little black devil.
sentences.i: Then in the middle of his field he caught sight of a heap of glowing coals, and when he went up to it full of wonder, there on top of the embers sat a little black devil.
sentences.n: erblicken is to catch sight of, a shade sharper than sehen. hinzugieng = hinzuging: the 1857 text writes gieng, fieng, hieng with -ie- throughout, and it is only a spelling. voll Verwunderung stands without an article, as German leaves such phrases bare.

sentences.t: „Du sitzest wohl auf einem Schatz?“ sprach das Bäuerlein.
sentences.l: “You are sitting, I suppose, on a treasure?” said the little-peasant.
sentences.i: “You will be sitting on a treasure, I dare say?” said the little peasant.
sentences.n: wohl in a question is not “well” but a guess: I suppose, I dare say. sitzest keeps the older full second-person ending where modern German writes sitzt.

sentences.t: „Ja wohl,“ antwortete der Teufel, „auf einem Schatz, der mehr Gold und Silber enthält als du dein Lebtag gesehen hast.“
sentences.l: “Yes indeed,” answered the devil, “on a treasure that contains more gold and silver than you have seen in all your life.”
sentences.i: “Indeed I am,” answered the devil, “on a treasure that holds more gold and silver than you have seen in all your days.”
sentences.n: ja wohl picks up the peasant’s wohl and turns the guess into a boast. dein Lebtag is an old accusative of time, for the whole of your life.

sentences.t: „Der Schatz liegt auf meinem Feld und gehört mir“ sprach das Bäuerlein.
sentences.l: “The treasure lies on my field and belongs to me,” said the little-peasant.
sentences.n: gehören takes the dative: gehört mir, belongs to me. The peasant’s claim is flat and legal, and the whole bargain follows from it.

sentences.t: „Er ist dein“ antwortete der Teufel, „wenn du mir zwei Jahre lang die Hälfte von dem gibst, was dein Acker hervorbringt: Geld habe ich genug, aber ich trage Verlangen nach den Früchten der Erde.“
sentences.l: “It is yours,” answered the devil, “if you give me for two years the half of that which your field brings forth: money I have enough, but I carry a longing for the fruits of the earth.”
sentences.i: “It is yours,” answered the devil, “if for two years you give me half of what your field brings forth. Money I have enough of, but I have a craving for the fruits of the earth.”
sentences.n: Er ist dein — er, he, because Schatz is masculine, where English must say “it”. Verlangen tragen nach is an elevated way of saying to long for; and the fronted Geld habe ich genug puts the emphasis exactly where the devil wants it.

sentences.t: Das Bäuerlein gieng auf den Handel ein.
sentences.l: The little-peasant went into the bargain.
sentences.i: The little peasant agreed to the bargain.
sentences.n: auf etwas eingehen is to agree to something, to close with an offer — a separable verb whose particle has travelled to the end of the clause: gieng … ein.

sentences.t: „Damit aber kein Streit bei der Theilung entsteht,“ sprach es, „so soll dir gehören was über der Erde ist und mir was unter der Erde ist.“
sentences.l: “But so that no quarrel arises at the dividing,” it said, “what is above the earth shall belong to you and what is under the earth to me.”
sentences.i: “But so that no quarrel arises over the dividing,” he said, “what is above the earth shall be yours, and what is under the earth mine.”
sentences.n: The whole tale turns on this sentence, so the literal keeps über der Erde and unter der Erde as the German has them — above the earth, under the earth — rather than saying anything about crops. sprach es: es, it, because Bäuerlein is a neuter diminutive, and the tale calls its hero it throughout. Theilung is the 1857 spelling of Teilung.

sentences.t: Dem Teufel gefiel das wohl, aber das listige Bäuerlein hatte Rüben gesät.
sentences.l: To the devil that was well pleasing, but the sly little-peasant had sown turnips.
sentences.i: That pleased the devil well enough, but the sly little peasant had sown turnips.
sentences.n: gefallen puts the person in the dative and the thing in the nominative — dem Teufel gefiel das, to the devil that was pleasing. Turnips grow under the earth, which settles the first year before it has begun.

sentences.t: Als nun die Zeit der Ernte kam, so erschien der Teufel und wollte seine Frucht holen, er fand aber nichts als die gelben welken Blätter, und das Bäuerlein, ganz vergnügt, grub seine Rüben aus.
sentences.l: When now the time of the harvest came, the devil appeared and wanted to fetch his crop, but he found nothing but the yellow withered leaves, and the little-peasant, quite delighted, dug out his turnips.
sentences.i: When the time of harvest came, the devil appeared and would fetch his crop; but he found nothing but the yellow withered leaves, while the little peasant, thoroughly pleased, dug up his turnips.
sentences.n: Frucht here is not fruit but the standing crop, whatever the field yields. welken is the adjective welk, withered, inflected — not the verb welken, to wither. grub … aus is ausgraben, dug out, with the particle at the end.

sentences.t: „Einmal hast du den Vortheil gehabt,“ sprach der Teufel, „aber für das nächstemal soll das nicht gelten. Dein ist was über der Erde wächst und mein was darunter ist.“
sentences.l: “This once you have had the advantage,” said the devil, “but for the next time that shall not hold. Yours is what grows above the earth and mine what is under it.”
sentences.i: “This once you have had the advantage,” said the devil, “but next time that shall not stand. Yours is what grows above the earth, and mine what is below.”
sentences.n: gelten is to be valid, to hold good, of a bargain. das nächstemal is an accusative of time, the next time, printed as one word in 1857. The devil reverses the two halves and is sure he has learnt his lesson.

sentences.l: “Right by me too,” answered the little-peasant.
sentences.i: “That suits me,” answered the little peasant.
sentences.n: mir auch recht is elliptical — das ist mir auch recht, that is all right by me too. The peasant agrees at once, which ought to be warning enough.

sentences.t: Als aber die Zeit zur Aussat kam, säte das Bäuerlein nicht wieder Rüben, sondern Waitzen.
sentences.l: But when the time for the sowing came, the little-peasant sowed not turnips again, but wheat.
sentences.i: But when sowing-time came, the little peasant did not sow turnips again, but wheat.
sentences.n: Waitzen is the 1857 spelling of Weizen, wheat, and Aussat of Aussaat, the sowing. nicht … sondern is the German pair for “not … but”, sondern being reserved for what replaces the thing denied.

sentences.t: Die Frucht ward reif, das Bäuerlein gieng auf den Acker und schnitt die vollen Halme bis zur Erde ab.
sentences.l: The crop grew ripe, the little-peasant went onto the field and cut the full stalks off right down to the earth.
sentences.i: The crop ripened; the little peasant went out to the field and cut the full stalks off right down to the ground.
sentences.n: ward is the old simple past of werden, modern wurde; it turns up on every page of these tales. abschneiden, to cut off, with its particle at the end: schnitt … ab. Cutting bis zur Erde leaves the devil his half exactly, and nothing in it.

sentences.t: Als der Teufel kam, fand er nichts als die Stoppeln und fuhr wüthend in eine Felsenschlucht hinab.
sentences.l: When the devil came, he found nothing but the stubble and drove furiously down into a rocky ravine.
sentences.i: When the devil came he found nothing but the stubble, and went raging down into a rocky ravine.
sentences.n: wüthend is the 1857 spelling of wütend, raging. fuhr … hinab, from hinabfahren: the devil goes down where devils go, and the tale does not trouble to say more.

sentences.t: „So muß man die Füchse prellen“ sprach das Bäuerlein, gieng hin und holte sich den Schatz.
sentences.l: “So must one cheat the foxes,” said the little-peasant, went over and fetched himself the treasure.
sentences.i: “That is the way to cheat a fox,” said the little peasant, and he went and fetched the treasure for himself.
sentences.n: prellen is to cheat, to swindle; die Füchse prellen — to cheat the foxes — is a proverbial way of saying you have out-tricked the tricky. holte sich carries a dative of advantage: fetched it for himself.

glossary.bestellt: bestellen — tilled, worked (a field) (past participle; den Acker bestellen; elsewhere also to order, arrange)
glossary.dran: dran — = daran, at it, to it; ‘einen dran kriegen’ = to catch somebody out, to get the better of him
glossary.dämmerung: die Dämmerung — twilight, dusk (here of the evening)
glossary.es: es — it; also the pronoun for a person named by a neuter noun (‘sprach es’ = said the Bäuerlein)
glossary.gehören: gehören — to belong (infinitive, + dative: ‘soll dir gehören’ = shall belong to you)
glossary.gehört: gehören — belongs (3rd sg. present, + dative: ‘gehört mir’ = belongs to me); not gehört, heard
glossary.ja: ja — yes (‘ja wohl’ = yes indeed); also the flavouring particle, surely, after all
glossary.kleiner: klein — little, small (masc. nom.: ‘ein kleiner schwarzer Teufel’); the same form also serves as the comparative, smaller
glossary.narren: der Narr — fool (acc. sg. in the fixed phrase jemanden zum Narren haben: to make a fool of someone)
glossary.streichen: der Streich — tricks, pranks (dat. pl.; von seinen Streichen erzählen: to tell of his tricks)
glossary.welken: welk — withered, wilted (adj., inflected; die gelben welken Blätter)
glossary.wohl: wohl — well, indeed; in a question a guess: I suppose, I dare say (‘du sitzest wohl auf einem Schatz?’)
